en: The *Nyāyamukha-śāstra-vyākhyā* (Commentary on the Introduction to Logic), composed by Master Tai.

Regarding the initial statement "Nyāya" (*Inming*): among the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), it refers to the science of logic; that is, it is the general term for all treatises on logic (*hetuvidyā*).
This is the title.
*Nyāyamukha-śāstra* is an alternative designation for this treatise.
Regarding the first term, "cause" (hetu),
there are two kinds: the first is the productive cause (janana-hetu).
Second is the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*).
What is now being analyzed is precisely the revealing cause, while also analyzing the producing cause (*janana-hetu*) incidentally.
Within the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*), there are further three types.
The first is the "reason based on meaning" (*arthahetu*), which refers generally to that which is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
The meaning of "being produced" (kṛtakatva) is the logical reason (hetu).
As for the proponent's formulation: [text follows].
The statement regarding "the nature of being produced" is the third: the cause for knowledge,
which serves to refute all opposing disputants.
And for those who have realized the meaning,
they understand the preceding causes of meaning and causes of expression,
as well as the mind and mental factors.
Collectively, these are termed "wisdom.
These three causes are all capable of illuminating that sound is impermanent.
Just as a lamp illuminates objects,
it is therefore called "light.
This is a name derived from its objective referent.
"Clarity" (ming) refers to wisdom (jñāna).
Furthermore, this very clarity-wisdom is able to illuminate its causal object.
Having fully realized the fundamental principle, it is therefore called *hetuvidyā* (the science of reasons).
This means that the reason itself is the illumination; this is the verbal expression.
Regarding those called "Logicians" (Hetuvādins):
first, because they arise from logic (*hetuvidyā*),
they are named "Logicians" based on that very logic.
It is called *hetuvidyā* (logic) because it gives rise to knowledge;
thus, it is named *hetuvidyā* after its result. Alternatively, if the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*) refers to the object of knowledge, then it is the sphere of *hetuvidyā*.
Therefore, it is called Hetuvidyā (Logic).
Another explanation is that "hetu" (cause/reason) refers to the aforementioned endowment of the objects of knowledge.
"Elucidation" (ming) means "discrimination" (bian).
This treatise is called *Hetuvidyā* because it discriminates and elucidates this cause (*hetu*).
These two characters, *hetuvidyā* (logic),

are the name for the treatise on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). As for the term "correct reasoning" (*nyāya*), it refers to...
Wisdom illuminates principles.
It proceeds from names as the causes of principles,
for principles give rise to speech.
Speech is also called "principle" (li).
The object illuminated by wisdom is likewise called "principle."
If the principle exists, it is correct;
if it excludes [the incorrect], why call it "correct"?
This principle is the correct principle.
Only by using this treatise as a gateway can one attain awakening and understanding; therefore,
it is called the Gateway to Right Reasoning (*Nyāyamukha*).
Furthermore, another interpretation is that "Correct Reasoning" (Nyāya) refers to the fifty-odd treatises, such as the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*.
Because this treatise serves as a gateway to that [system],
it is called the *Nyāyamukha* (Gateway to Reasoning).
It was composed by the Lord of Devas (*Devanātha*) for those who enter into correct reasoning.
This treatise is named *Nyāya* (Right Principle).
One who is able to enter into it is said to have "entered into right principle" (*nyāyapraveśa*).
The character "wú" (無) is omitted;
it is like ascending the steps to approach the gate.
This is the title established by the Heavenly Lord (Indra).
Furthermore, it is like entering a room by way of its door;
this refers to what is called "name" (*nāman*) in this treatise.
Another interpretation is as follows:
"Right principle" (nyāya) refers to the principle of phenomena (dharmatā);
it is correct and not deviant.
Now, taking this treatise as the gateway,
it universally gives rise to correct wisdom and leads to the realization of the true principle; therefore,
it is named the "Gateway to True Principle" (Nyāyamukha).
Regarding "correct reasoning" (nyāya):
it refers to works such as the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* composed by the Bodhisattva Dignāga,
which elucidate the correct principles of all phenomena.
This treatise and that treatise serve as gateways for entering [the path]. As for *Taiyoku Ryū* (太域龍):

in its original phonetics, it is *Mahāsthāmaprāpta* (*Mahā* being pronounced with the *da* and *li* tones, followed by *na* in the departing tone; *sthāma* here means "great," *prāpta* means "attained," and *nāga* means "dragon"). This refers to the Bodhisattva.
Like a dragon of a great region, it is named for its possession of great majesty and power.
"For those who desire," etc.: this refers to this entire treatise.
It consists of three parts.
This present treatise is the section on the introduction and the occasion for its composition.
Following the section on the second thesis and the subsequent discourse,
the main body of the treatise (*śāstrakāya*) is explained;
thirdly, there are the four lines at the conclusion of the treatise.
This is the section on manifesting that which accords with reality.
From antiquity, there have been ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika),
as well as the various vehicles of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Each has formulated their own system of *hetuvidyā* (logic), and both have presented their respective positions for establishing and refuting.
Now, I wish to address the meaning of those establishments and refutations.
To simplify the discourse on wisdom:
grasp the reality that wisdom arises from luminosity.
Either taking what is not a fault to be a fault,
or taking what is a fault to be not a fault;
now, by means of discerning wisdom, one clearly distinguishes that this grasping of faults as faults is indeed a fault.
Regarding the statement "it is not an error, it is not an error":
this means that both the *sādhana* (the proof) and the *dūṣaṇa* (the refutation) that appear similar are termed *sādhana*.
The refutation of the *sādhana* by the *dūṣaṇa* is what constitutes the true meaning.
It is not the case that there is no fault in taking [the thesis] unilaterally when establishing or refuting;
the single phrase "the thesis and so forth" is as explained elsewhere.
Among these, that which reaches the name "thesis" (pakṣa) is of four kinds.
Regarding all remaining positions,
such as the statement "the blue lotus has fragrance," this is not established because it entails the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
Regarding the two types of propositions (*pakṣa*) that have been studied:
the first is not established because it entails the fault of contradicting one's own doctrine (*sva-śāstra*) from the outset;
the third is the proposition as such (*artha-mātra*).
For example, when establishing that sound is impermanent,
it is merely empty and selfless;
because it is not what was originally intended to be established, it is not so established.
Fourth is the school that follows one's own intention;
furthermore, it establishes the doctrines of other teachings within its own school.
Therefore, there is no fault.
This is explained in detail elsewhere.
If one holds that [the object] is removed by the arrival of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇaprāpti*), the thesis has five faults.
This refers to the contradiction between the name and the meaning.
Because these five faults constitute a contradiction between the meaning and the thesis (*pakṣa*),
this is the contradiction in meaning.
That which can dispel [the provisional] and cause the ultimate to be established— because it is not of a nature contrary to that [ultimate]—
is called the "authentic thesis" (*siddhānta*).
Since the thesis leads to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), it is similar to the explanation of the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Therefore, regarding that which constitutes the "proof" (sādhana), [the author] cites various treatises composed by Vasubandhu;
he establishes that a single reason, two reasons, or many words constitute the proof,
thereby corroborating the preceding text.
The *Vādavidhi* and so forth include,
by extension, the *Vādanyāya* and the *Vādahṛdaya*.
These three treatises were all composed by Vasubandhu.
Regarding the treatises on inference such as those by Bhāviveka and others, all take one reason and two examples as the means of proof (*sādhana*).

As for the statement that "the words [of the thesis] constitute the nature of the proof": in the verse, the three words beginning with "the subject" (*pakṣa*) are collectively termed the means of proof.
This is to demonstrate that a single reason and two examples together constitute the nature of a complete proof (*sādhana*).
It is like a house, which is formed by the collective assembly of many things such as rafters, beams, walls, and doors.
It cannot be that because the rafters and so forth are prior [to the house], the house would also be many.

For this reason, an instance that results in the fallacy of "reaching" (prāpti) is deficient in one of the three members of the syllogism—namely, the thesis (pakṣa), the reason (hetu), or the example (dṛṣṭānta).
Regarding the fault of the nature of the proof (*sādhana*), prior to Dignāga,
if it was said that the thesis (*pakṣa*) was deficient;
Alternatively, failing to provide either the reason (*hetu*) or the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) as required is termed a fault of the proof (*sādhanadoṣa*).
One master explains it thus:
There may be a thesis but no reason or example;
there may be a reason but no thesis or example;
and there may be an example but no thesis or reason.
There are three types of statements:
those that have a thesis and a reason but lack an example;
those that have a thesis and an example but lack a reason; and [those that have all three].
There is a case where there is a reason and an example, but no thesis;
the reason and example constitute the seventh proposition.
Such are the seven propositions.
This is called the fault of deficiency in the proof (*sādhana*).
Furthermore, another master explains:
"The previous statement may be so."
The seventh case cannot be accepted.
If there were one or two minor deficiencies remaining, one might speak of "deficiency" (*ūna*);
however, in the seventh position, both the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are entirely absent.
What is meant by "deficiency"?
Therefore, it is not permissible. Dignāga said:
However, within the proof (*sādhana*) consisting of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), there is the fault of deficiency (*nyūnatā*).
Regarding this, Bhadanta Śrīlāta previously explained that there exists a reason (*hetu*) that possesses neither a similar nor a dissimilar instance.

There are cases where there is a similar instance (sapakṣa) but no reason (hetu) and no dissimilar instance (vipakṣa); cases where there is a dissimilar instance but no reason and no similar instance;
and cases where both are lacking, forming three propositions. Furthermore, there are cases where there is a reason and a similar instance but no dissimilar instance.
There is a case where there is a similar instance but no dissimilar instance and no reason; there is a case where there is a dissimilar instance and a reason which is itself the similar instance;
and there is a case where one [of these] is missing, resulting in three propositions.
There are two analogies regarding intrinsic existence and the absence of causes,
which constitute the seventh case.
After the Dharma Master had previously explained "substantiality" (*sat*), he [proceeded].
A seventh alternative is not established,
as previously demonstrated.
To say that this constitutes a fault in the proof (*sādhana*) means:
This is merely an interpretation of the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "because it reaches therein," the commentary states:
this is the opening of a branch-discourse.
In this manner, the phrases "now," "if," "as for," "only," and so forth, which are words expressing desire for a branch [of the argument],
explain the meaning of the first thesis-statement;
therefore, it says, "among these."
The subsequent commentary states:
"Within this collection of multiple terms, such as the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth, the locus (*dharmin*),
reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are excluded."
They uphold their respective tenets; thus,
each is "the middle" [of its own system],
because they grasp the specific [view] by raising up [and holding] their own position.
It is called "is" (*asti*) because it occurs within the context of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth; alternatively,
it serves to distinguish and maintain [the subject].
To simplify and eliminate extremes while maintaining the adoption of the Middle Way:
to regard what resembles the fallacies of the thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*) as being authentic is called "augmentation" (*samāropa*).
The True Sect (Shinshū), by means of parables, asserts that what is not true is termed "deficiency" (son).
It avoids these two extremes and upholds the Middle Way.
This refers to the section on "the true name" within the aforementioned discussion of establishing and refuting the capacity for meaning.
Question: If a mantra that is not a true name is considered a defect, why is it not likewise so for a word that is not a true likeness?
Answer: "True" refers to that which is not truly the correct principle for delivering sentient beings; thus it is termed "diminution.
"Resemblance" refers to that which is not a resemblance of the method for delivering them; since it is irrational, it is not termed "reduction.
Alternatively, both may be attributed to the treatise itself.
Question: Since this text explains the True Doctrine (shinjō), why is it that here it also describes that which resembles the Middle Way?
Answer: It is stated in the fourth line of the verse:
It should be understood that the first three phrases serve to exclude those that resemble the thesis (pakṣābhāsa) by means of the meaning of what is incompatible with it.
The commentary contains general statements regarding the real and the semblance.
Furthermore, it explains the meaning of the phrase "among these."
However, in the True Sect (Shingon) and other traditions, it is likewise so;
for since the verse states that what is to be established is called the "thesis" (*pakṣa*), [it follows accordingly].
The thesis stated in the preceding sentence of the treatise cannot be refuted by its contradictory meaning;
it cannot be refuted by that contradictory meaning.
If it is argued that the preceding phrase also applies to what resembles a thesis (*pratijñā*),
then the following phrase should likewise apply to both the real and the resembling.
Regarding the statement "among these, such as the thesis (pakṣa) and so forth":
the three— thesis, reason (hetu), and example (dṛṣṭānta)—
are all free from the two extremes of addition and subtraction.
This means that within this [state], one abandons the extremes of increase and decrease and adopts the Middle Way;
therefore, it is called "the middle."
Alternatively, it may be understood as selecting from among the three [categories], such as the "correct thesis" (*sādhya*) and so forth;
hence the expression "among these.
As for the phrase "only taking," etc., it is intended to exclude the knowledge of the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
One may either understand the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) by setting aside the thesis (*pakṣa*), or one may discern the thesis by setting aside the reason and the example.
The term "differentiation" (*viniścaya*) signifies the meaning of exclusion.
If one were merely to re-explain the meaning of the preceding "exclusion and retention," one should likewise say "exclusion and selection" (*viniyoga*).
It is not merely discerning knowledge.

The second [meaning] of "to discern" (vī-) refers to *pravicaya* (discriminative investigation). This *vicaya* (investigation) consists of selecting the correct and rejecting the incorrect; it is not simply knowledge.
This means that if it is the *pakṣa* (the thesis), it is a selection;
if it is the *sādhana* (the proof), it is a discernment.
"Distinct" (*bhinna*) has the meaning of "different."
It is also understood as taking [the thesis] separately; that is, one takes the thesis separately from the reason and the example.
If that is so, since the term "discrimination" (vikalpa) already implies this, why is it necessary to specify it separately?
The answer is: the name "discrimination" is a general term.
Here, "to discern" (jian) means to distinguish; it does not refer to "to select and retain" (jianchi) and so forth.
Therefore, the word "distinct" (bie) is used again.
Regarding the establishment [of a thesis] according to one's own intention, there are four types of propositions (*pakṣa*),
as explained previously. The fourth is the proposition established according to one's own preference (*svābhiprāya-pakṣa*).
Just as Sapoda has already demonstrated his eloquence,
he does not contradict the tenets of the three preceding treatises within his own school.
Following his own inclinations,
he falsely assumed the role of another teacher and established the doctrines of that other teaching.
The name is established according to one’s own intention;
thus, there is no fault.
The treatise states that "belonging to" (shǔwéi) is the term for the thesis (*pakṣa*), while "action" (*yè*) consists of two characters.
The term "pseudo" (*sadṛśa*) excludes pseudo-reasons and pseudo-examples;
the two characters "established" (*sādhya*) exclude true reasons and true examples.
Regarding the statement that "desire" is what is to be established:
proponents merely intend to establish it through their own desire.
The proponent merely intends to establish the thesis through mental action; because he desires to establish the meaning of the thesis,
it is called "that which is intended to be established."
This is the original intention of the proponent (*vādin*).
Since the true reason (*hetu*) and the true example (*dṛṣṭānta*) have already been established through prior refutation,
they do not take pleasure in being the nature of that which proves (*sādhana*).
If one were to speak of "pleasure" in a manner different from this,
one would merely state that which is established as the thesis (*pakṣa*),
thereby excluding the true reason (*hetu*) and example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Regarding the nature of proof (*sādhana*):
it refers to that which establishes the probandum (*sādhya*), as well as fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) and fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*).
It must further be established;
it should also consume its own thesis. Nevertheless, although it is that which is to be established, [it would still entail this consequence].
This is not what the proponent originally intended;
although it is something established,
it is not the thesis (*pakṣa*).
Regarding the statement that the semblance of a reason further establishes [the point],
there are two types of theories in the science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*).
The first establishes that sound arises from conditions and is not subject to extinction.
Second, they establish that sound merely manifests from conditions and is neither produced nor extinguished;
for example, when a Buddhist disciple debates with a proponent of the science of grammar (śabda-vidyā),
he establishes the thesis that sound is impermanent.
The reason "because of being produced" has the atom as its similar instance (sapakṣa). This reason,
with respect to the proponent who maintains that sound is manifest (abhivyaktivādin), [is unestablished].
There is the fallacy of one or the other being unestablished (*anyatarāsiddha*),
because that opponent does not admit that sound is a product (*kṛtakatva*).
That reason must further be established:
sound is a product because it is maintained as a real entity by conditions; this is the reason.
It is like the common examples of a jar and so forth;
furthermore, the opponent does not accept the example of the atom as being impermanent.
There is the fault that the thesis is not established;
however, it must further be established that the atom is impermanent.
Thesis: [The subject] possesses resistance because it has the property of being obstructive; the reason is "because it has the property of being obstructive";
the concordant example is "just like a jar," and so forth.
The Śābdika masters establish that atoms are eternal because they possess resistance;
such is their reason and example.
At the time when perception is established,
although it is that which is to be established, such is the intention of the proponent.
At that time, he delighted only in establishing the fundamental tenets;
he did not delight in establishing fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) or fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*). Furthermore, it is explained as follows:
The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that which is intended to be established;
it is called a "thesis" because it is that which is to be proven.
That is to say, taking "not desiring" as the reason and the example fails to establish the reason and the example;
if one were to take something other than "desiring" as the thesis to be established.
Now, regarding that which is capable of establishing [the probandum],

it is explained that the pseudo-reason (*hetvābhāsa*) and pseudo-example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) constitute the nature of the means of establishment (*sādhanatva*), whether they are unestablished or further established.
It should also be called a thesis (*pakṣa*);
however, although the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) and fallacious example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) may be further established [as such], they are not so.
At the time of its attainment, it is solely of the nature of the means of establishment (*sādhana*), and not the thesis (*pakṣa*) to be established; therefore,
one should know that "desire" (*iṣṭa*) constitutes the thesis as that which is to be established.
It is not intended to establish [a valid thesis].
Rather, it establishes what appear to be reasons and examples as being the thesis itself.
The establishment of the reason and the example is as previously explained.
This passage belongs within the section on "Entering into Principle" (*tattvapraveśa*).

It is composed according to the author's own preference; however, this passage lacks a commonly established subject (*dharmin*), because the property (*dharma*)—namely, "the nature of being a specific distinction"—is not itself commonly established.
The Master of Treatises explains:
"Śaṅkara does not delight in this treatise,
just as the Sāṃkhya does not delight in the Śākya-putrīyas."
Establishing the vehicle is an act of grace.
This is because it commits the fallacy of the unestablished basis (*āśrayāsiddha*) within the reason (*hetu*),
for a reason must necessarily be established upon a factual locus (*dharmin*).
Since the phenomenon [under discussion] does not exist,
the reason (hetu) established is unproven;
this is solely because the opponent does not believe me.
Thus, one establishes the vehicle of the abandonment of what is to be transcended.
This is called the "extremely established qualifier," as when the Buddha, in response to the arguments of the cowherds, established that sound is impermanent and subject to affliction.
This is inherently the fault of lacking a similar instance (sapakṣa),
because the Sāṃkhya school does not admit the existence of phenomena that undergo cessation through affliction.
Therefore, there is no analogy.
It is solely because one does not believe that sound possesses the affliction of cessation that one establishes the vehicle based on the cessation of affliction.
Cessation is also that which is transcended.
Regarding the nature of meaning:
it is like establishing a thesis by stating that "sound is impermanent."
Regarding the distinction between impermanence and sound as characteristics of sensation,
the definitive statement must be thus.
Why should one further employ words of distinction to effect a distinction? Therefore,
this treatise consists of sentences that are beyond comparison.
The treatise states: "In order to manifest the ultimate meaning, [the proponent] refutes [the opponent's position].

This means that the theses established by other non-Buddhists and the like involve five kinds of faults. Now, in order to demonstrate how one may avoid the faults inherent in the theses established by those other non-Buddhists and the like, [the author proceeds].
Therefore, there is the statement of the fourth alternative.
One may also establish that "this thesis is faultless" while others are faulty;
now, I wish to clarify the exclusion of those other faulty theses.
Therefore, these words were spoken.
As for the statement that "it is not the case that the meaning is negated by contradicting those [characteristics]," this refers to the explicit text.
It is simply that the word "able" (or "capable") is omitted.
As for the meaning of "contradiction," it refers to the fact that the thesis contradicts its own fundamental tenet.
The meaning of being contrary to what is accepted as food is precisely this true thesis;
it is not subverted by a fallacious thesis.
Therefore, it is said that "non-contradiction" is the meaning;
that which can dispel the meaning of words is precisely the meaning of contradiction.
"Speech-sound" refers to the meaning that is expressed.
"Eliminating" means to refute or dispel.
This is one sense [of the term].
Entering into the theory, [one finds] there is no [such thing].
Although the preceding [argument] took "karma" as the probandum (*sādhya*),
the thesis (*pakṣa*) has still not been established.
One must necessarily understand these five faults before one can establish a school;
what follows below demonstrates that [the opponent's position] violates the meaning and cannot resolve these issues.
The treatise states: "If it is not that which is dispatched by direct perception, then the verbal expression that contradicts the meaning is precisely free from the five faults.
This refers to the meaning indicated by the words of the True Doctrine."
Because it contradicts a faulty thesis,
it is called "contradictory meaning" (*viruddhārtha*).
If there is a faulty thesis...
Thus, that which possesses faults is set aside by the true meaning of its opposite;
if there is no fault,
it is set aside by the true thesis of its opposite.
If this very thesis is not excluded by those five types of faulty theses,
it is called a "true thesis.
This occurs within the context of comparing and substituting these five types of faulty theses.
When one is able to dispatch [the mind],
the True Principle (zhenzong) is that which is dispatched.
Below, the ability to dispatch is brought forth.
This reveals whether this [system] can or cannot dispel the True Doctrine (tattvārtha).
Furthermore, it is explained that this is because the doctrine is compared with the True Doctrine.
It is not that which is to be negated,
because it would entail a logical fallacy;
therefore, it is said that it is not negated by the verbal expression whose meaning is contrary to it.
This means that the True Doctrine (zhenzong) has something it dispatches.
Below, five faults are raised to examine this True Doctrine;
it is merely that which is dispatched.
This demonstrates that it is not those [other positions] which are capable of refuting [the thesis].
This is the explanation of the fourth line of the verse.
The treatise says: "If one establishes [a position] such as 'this is false,' this is the fault of self-contradiction in one's own words."
It refers to certain non-Buddhists who maintain that all speech is entirely unreal; thus,
the very speech they utter contradicts their own position.
Why is that? If you say that all speech is false,
is the speech from your own mouth real or false?
If you say this is true,
for what reason do you say that everything is false speech?
If you yourself say it is false, [how can you claim otherwise]?
Then all speech would necessarily be true.
If you further attempt to defend this by saying,
"One must understand the meaning of what is spoken from my mouth," [the response follows].
Regarding the statement that "all other speech is false":
suppose there is a second person who hears what you have said— that all speech is false—
and immediately speaks again.
What you have said is true.
When that person utters speech,
is it false or is it real?
If you say it is false,
then your words are empty;
if you say it is true, [then...]
Why do you immediately say, "except for what I have said"?
If you further attempt to defend yourself by saying,
"Except for the Path, my words regarding this one person are true," [then...]
All awakenings, when analyzed, are entirely false.
If that is so, then the third person who asserts that the speech of this second person is also true must likewise exist.
Regarding these words of the third person:
are they false or true?
If one says they are false, [then...]
If the words of both this second person and the first person are true, they must be false.
If the words of the third person are true,
why does he say, "excluding myself and this person"?
"Is it otherwise false?
The treatise states: "Alternatively, that which arrives first is eternal. This contradicts one's own teaching;
it is also termed a contradiction with one's own tenet (*svasiddhāntavirodha*).
Within the school of the owl-like philosophers (Ulūka),
they first establish that sound is non-existent,
yet they further establish that sound is eternal.
Thus, within one's own school, it contradicts what was previously established.
The treatise says: "Furthermore, if [it is argued] that it exists because it is co-existent [with the object], this contradicts worldly consensus."
That is to say, regarding the thesis that is being established,
[a reason] is "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) because,
for example, the moon is "only that which possesses a rabbit."
This month receives those phenomena of the same class that have no remainder;
since these phenomena do not exist in other months,
it is therefore called "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*).
Furthermore, it is a cause because its nature is as it has been heard;
this cause is unique, for it is a unique property (asādhāraṇadharma).
